thread.title: Stocks to Buy in China's Slowing Economy

title: Stocks to Buy in China's Slowing Economy
text:
Stocks to Buy in China’s Slowing Economy By Jan. 24, 2019 6:00 a.m. ET Order Reprints Illustration by Joan Wong Text size
The news out of China is gloomy—and likely to get worse. Perversely, that could bring global markets a respite as the slowdown puts more pressure on Beijing to strike a trade deal with the U.S. and pushes its leaders to offer more stimulus. But investors should tread carefully: China isn’t just trying to jump-start its economy; it’s trying to create a new economy—which will entail risk while opening up new long-term investment opportunities.
China’s economy isn’t imploding, but the days of 10% growth are behind it. Economists expect growth of roughly half that pace—possibly less. The slowdown comes as China tries to wean itself from debt-fueled investments in infrastructure, housing, and other fixed assets and attempts to grow beyond its role as the world’s factory to generate more sustainable growth from domestic consumption and technology innovation . These latter factors will produce the next generation of winning investments.
The trade war and slowing global growth have complicated the shift. To prevent too-swift a slowdown, China already has backed off some steps it was taking to reduce its debt by restraining credit growth and increasing regulation. Those steps and the trade uncertainty have sapped business confidence.
“In my 18 years in China, I have never seen the level of nervousness and pessimism that I have seen in the past nine months,” says Michael Pettis, a professor of finance at Peking University’s Guanghua School of Management and a nonresident senior fellow at the Carnegie Asia Program. But, he adds, “This is a good thing, not a bad thing. Ordinary Chinese people are fully aware that there must be changes in the way the economy is managed. The biggest opposition that [President] Xi Jinping faces is likely to be from local vested interests.”
Cheap valuations following 2018’s awful stock market performance and hopes of a U.S. trade deal have drawn investors back into emerging market stock funds, which have seen 14 consecutive weeks of net inflows—the longest streak in 16 months, according to EPFR Global. The iShares MSCI China exchange-traded fund (ticker: MCHI) is up 5.5% this year.
But, wary of U.S.-China tensions and restructuring risks, fund managers are picking their spots carefully. Portfolio managers are focusing on companies that can prosper from—or at least weather—the shifts in the economy and changes in consumer preferences, as well as the companies operating in the areas that China is investing in for its future, like technology and health care.
Whatever China’s “new normal” growth is, the economy is slowing and wage growth—key for spending—is softening, with disposable income for urban residents rising just 5.6% last year, from 6.5% in 2017. That is a major change for a generation of Chinese who have known only rising incomes and growth, says Justin Leverenz, who manages the $38 billion, top-performing Oppenheimer Developing Markets fund (ODMAX). He been buying Chinese stocks in the selloff but remains underweight because of the risks.
Investors in China face their own paradigm shift, as former engines of growth like the property market—and ancillary sectors like financials and real estate—slow, Leverenz says. Auto and appliance sales have been clobbered and may not fully recover, since property, auto, and appliance purchases tend to go together, Leverenz says. The same goes for material companies if China leans less on debt-fueled investments.
Instead, Leverenz is focusing on companies that make up the “new China” and are the key technological innovators and service providers for the economy’s transition. That includes companies using technology to disrupt or create new industries, like recently public Meituan Dianping (3690.Hong Kong), which derives part of its business from food delivery and the rest from being what Leverenz describes as “the Alibaba for services,” helping bricks-and-mortar companies with marketing, supply chain, and customer-relationship management. “These companies are about taking market share from less-efficient players. Lower GDP growth does not have the same dramatic impact on them as ‘old China’ companies [for which] profit cycles are tied to pricing and deflation is now the worry,” Leverenz says.
Services have been a bright spot in China’s economic data, with a private market survey in December showing its strongest growth since June. Tiffany Hsiao, co-manager of Matthews China Small Companies (MCSMX) fund, sees big potential in Chinese software companies behind services, like cloud computing and big data provider Kingdee International Software (0268.Hong Kong). “There is tremendous opportunity for those providing software to improve productivity or helping with recruiting, and we see growth there despite all the uncertainty,” Hsiao says. Investors and global companies alike have chased after China’s consumers. Near term, economic weakness and layoffs could dent household income and curtail spending, but consumption growth is expected to be on par with that of the U.S. and Western Europe combined through 2030, according to a recent McKinsey Global Institute report.
Consumer preferences, though, are changing. For example, consumers are increasingly spending more on services, like private education , travel, and even beauty treatments. Consumers are also less fixated on buying marquee brands to showcase their wealth, especially if a cheaper product offers the same functionality—as was the case recently with Apple (AAPL). While the iPhone is seen as a fashion statement, Leverenz says the products of Chinese companies like privately held Huawei and Xiaomi (1810.Hong Kong) are more commonly found in the pockets of mainstream consumers. Chinese rivals are also gaining ground in lodging. U.S. chains and multinationals invested aggressively in China, targeting the affluent, but now face high vacancy rates and little pricing power, Leverenz says. Meanwhile, local companies like Huazhu Group ’s (HTHT) China Lodging focused on the much bigger pool of more price-sensitive customers and are seeing strong growth.
The Chinese are also willing to pay more for quality on some items. “A decade ago, I wouldn’t have thought Chinese consumers would be buying music and movies. Fake DVDs were everywhere. But they are now paying for high-quality streaming content,” says Michael Oh, manager of the Matthews Asia Innovators fund (MATFX). One holding is iQiyi (IQ), a video-streaming company that Oh compares to Netflix (NFLX).
To get consumers to spend more of their savings to boost consumption, China has to help create safety nets by supporting education and health care. Expanding universal health care is one of the government’s big priorities, as a quarter of its population will be over 60 by 2030. “Chinese companies positioning themselves to address domestic issues will be the most successful,” says Alberto Fassinotti, who oversees $3 billion in assets as a portfolio manager for emerging markets at Rock Creek Group. He has used the selloff to focus on such companies, with holdings including drugmaker China Medical System Holdings (0867.Hong Kong) and medical-device maker Shandong Weigao Group Medical Polymer (1066.Hong Kong).
China’s transition comes with plenty of risk. While China’s debt problem weighs heavily on the market, Fassinotti and others worry about unemployment if the services industry is unable to absorb the layoffs in manufacturing. “It is putting inordinate pressure on Xi to get this fixed,” Fassinotti says. “Our biggest concern is that his own allies start to turn against him if they see their interests threatened by this slowdown.”
Over the short term, those risks could put more pressure on Chinese officials to support the economy with a trade deal, more stimulus—or both. But kicking the can down the road only makes China’s debt more dangerous—a reason those buying Chinese stocks are going slow.
